utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber observed and was further informed about inappropriate interaction between the public gallery and Mr. Mladic. Now, I'm refraining from any observation as who initiated that, whether that was the public gallery or whether that was you, Mr. Mladic - it may have been both. We are not going to -- you are hinting it was the public gallery. Now, the best way of not having to respond to that is just to focus on what happens in this courtroom rather than to look at the public gallery. The Chamber at this moment doesn't find it necessary to put any measure in place, but if it would continue - and I'm therefore also addressing the public gallery - that if interaction is sought, whether from the public gallery or from the courtroom, that the solution would be to put a screen between Mr. Mladic and the public gallery so as to avoid, in whatever direction, such inappropriate interactions. So therefore, please refrain from it. And, Mr. Mladic, you can protect yourself if there would be any initiative from the public gallery, you can -- by focusing on what Mr. Groome is telling us or by focusing on what happens in the courtroom, there will be less reason to respond if anything would be there. Then, Mr. Groome, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, just prior to the break I was discussing the JNA's involvement in the events during the spring of 1992. Now before you on slide 43 is a report from the JNA, reporting how the JNA and its armed units, created and co-ordinated by the SDS, have worked together to take over the town of Vlasenica or "liberated," to use the reporter's term. The willingness of individual commanders to engage JNA troops and resources on the Serb side was watched carefully by senior Serb politicians, like Milosevic and Karadzic. As the time drew near to build a Bosnian Serb army, the officers selected from the JNA ranks to lead it were chosen in part because they had already demonstrated their competence and commitment to the goal of creating a Bosnian Serb state using military might. During this entire period, forces of the Territorial Defence or reserve units were subordinated to the JNA and then the VRS. Similarly, the Bosnian Serb police were also at different times working closely with the JNA and the VRS, and in some instances were formally subordinated to them. As Karadzic would say in 1995: "Gentlemen, we got the officers we asked for. I asked for Mladic." The choice of Mladic as commander wasn't a random one. Karadzic chose Mladic because he believed him to be an excellent officer capable of commanding the planned Bosnian Serb army, and because Karadzic believed he was willing to commit the crimes needed to achieve the strategic goals of Bosnian Serb leaders. In this particular entry from Mladic's military notebooks on slide 45, we can see that Mr. Mladic recorded the comments of JNA General Momcilo Perisic at a meeting in which there is a discussion of Mladic as a commander for a Bosnian Serb army. He records Perisic as saying that Perisic and Ninkovic undertook an initiative with Karadzic for Mladic to command the new Bosnian Serb army. Mladic records Perisic as saying: "You have the right person. If you support him, you will get what you want." You will get what you want. What they wanted was someone who would reinforce their hold on territories taken to date and advance the strategic goals already being implemented. On the 12th of May, 1992, when the VRS was established, the JNA withdrew from Bosnia. The JNA left behind most of its weapons and thousands of troops to the just-established VRS. It continued to pay the salaries of nearly the entire VRS officer corps, including Mladic, Galic, Krstic, Talic, and other senior officers you will learn about in this trial. The Prosecution will lead evidence establishing that within hours of the creation of the VRS it was able to adapt the communications systems and the command and control systems of the JNA. The Main Staff of the VRS was able to effectively issue commands and receive reports from subordinate units within hours. Slide 46 depicts the senior leadership of the VRS. The top row identifies the members of its Main Staff, and the second row the commanders of the six corps and its air force. A more complete organisational chart depicting the structure of the VRS can be found on page 28 of the Prosecution pre-trial brief. On the copy now before you, the 1st Krajina Corps, the Drina Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and the East Bosnia Corps are marked in red. These are the corps that are most relevant to the indictment. A comprehensive chronology of Mr. Mladic's professional career can also be found in the pre-trial brief at page 24. I will now describe some of the crimes for which Mr. Mladic is charged, crimes directly perpetrated by soldiers under his command. I will not discuss all of the crimes or describe them in any particular detail. I will mention just a few to illustrate in a general sense the types of crimes that were committed. I will use the strategic objectives as a framework and will begin with the second objective. I am leaving the first objective until the end because it permeates the others. There was a large concentration of Serbs in the Krajina prior to the war. Bosnian Serb leaders recognised that if this population was to be a viable part of a Bosnian Serb state, it had to be physically connected to it. The second objective was to create this physical connection. The indictment specifically enumerates crimes which occurred in five municipalities. Although not all within the corridor, they are all related to this particular objective: Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, Banja Luka, and Kotor Varos. Two of the most important municipalities in the Krajina were Prijedor and Sanski Most. Both had Muslim majorities and were adjacent to Banja Luka, a municipality with a strong Serb majority. The initial take-over of the two municipalities took place in April of 1992. These municipalities would see some of the worst ethnic cleansing. The JNA played a significant part in the initial take-over of the municipalities. Then-Colonel Momir Talic, one of Mladic's most trusted officers, personally participated in the take-over of Sanski Most. A few weeks later, after the creation of the VRS, Talic would be responsible for brutal attacks against Muslims in Prijedor. At the end of May, shortly after Mladic assumed the position of commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, approximately 50 soldiers set up howitzers and shelled the villages of Hrstuvo and Vrhpolje in Sanski Most. They returned the next week to burn the non-Serb house. They captured about 20 boys and men, marched them to Vrhpolje bridge, made them strip and then jump from the bridge. They shot each of the men as they entered the water. May I draw your attention to a weekly report from the security services centre now shown on slide 48. The security services centre is the regional headquarters of the police in Western Bosnia and was located in Banja Luka. It describes the retaliatory attack against the civilian population after two Serb soldiers were killed: "The army carried out an artillery attack on the village of Hambarine and mopped up the area." "... the army engaged in a mopping-up operation. Several hundred inhabitants of these villages were killed or wounded." On the 1st of June in Kljuc, the Bosnian Serb army completed the shelling and the ransacking of villages in the area of Velagici, a bombardment that lasted approximately four days. An order was given for all Muslim men near the Velagici school to come to the police station. About 77 unarmed men assembled there. Again, in a process that would be repeated throughout the conflict, they were forced to remove their valuables, their identifications, and were murdered there in front of the school -- I'm sorry, in front of the police station. Slide 49 is a report from Talic to his superiors at the Main Staff. It is dated the 14th of June, 1992. Here Talic informs Mladic that the greatest difficulty they face is not armed resistance, the most difficult situation they face is that there are now security and logistical problems because efforts to expel refugees have failed. They failed to expel all of the targeted population because of problems with buses and the fact that some people refused to leave their homes. If I can return to Kljuc for a moment, it is also a good example of how Mladic monitored the progress of the ethnic cleansing campaign. On the 8th of January, 1992, here shown on slide 50, Mladic notes that the ethnic population of Kljuc is comprised of 17.000 Muslims and 3.000 Croats. Once again at this point in time Mr. Mladic is based in Knin, Croatia. Slide 51 is from Mladic's military notebook and records a report he received from Jovo Banjac, president of Kljuc municipality. Banjac told him that there used to be 17.000 Muslims in Kljuc, now there are only 5.000. Mladic went on to note that he was told that 1500 people had departed that very day, the 11th of September, 1992. Slide 52 shows the next report he receives on progress in Kljuc municipality. It is about seven weeks after the last report. Here the number of Muslims has been further reduced to 2.000. In slide 53 we see a document from the 1st of July, 1992, only six weeks into Mladic's stewardship of the VRS. In it he pays tribute to the successes of Serb forces cleansing the area: "I'd like to pay tribute and express my gratitude to all soldiers, commanding officers of the 1st Krajina Corps and Eastern Bosnia Corps, members of air force and anti-aircraft defence of the Serbian Republic of BiH army as well as civilian Serbian population in the combat activity zone for successfully organised and implemented operation for breakthrough, expansion, and cleansing of corridor in Bosanska Posavina, between Eastern and Western Bosnia, as well as excogitation and organised joint action and co-ordination of combat units activities." On 10 July 1992, almost two months after Mladic took command, VRS soldiers surrounded the village of Brkici in Kljuc. Men between 16 and 60 were separated from their families and detained in a nearby meadow. They were marched to the elementary school in Biljani. Once preparations for killing them were in place, they were loaded in groups of five into a bus. The bus was driven to a field and as the men were forced off the bus they could see the bodies of those killed before them. They were murdered as they left the bus. A survivor will describe that day, how he threw himself to the ground and pretended to be dead. As he lay there, he heard the sound of earth-moving equipment. Another survivor of this massacre will describe during the trial hearing one of the soldiers comment to another, "It's all going according to plan." By the end of July 1992, just ten weeks after the Bosnian Serb army was created, General Talic considered that he had completed his task. Slide 54, now on the screen before you, is a report of the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 24th of July, 1992. We read: "We have liberated the territories we consider our own." The territory being referred to was land upon which people of several ethnicities lived, farming their lands, raising their children, land forcibly taken, the rightful owners murdered or thrown into detention camps, forced to leave the area. The report goes on to describe that a centuries' old aspiration has been fulfilled, one referred to in modern times as strategic objective number two. On the screens before you on slide 55 is a report from the archives of the 1st Krajina Corps, reporting on what happened in Grabovica to Elvedin Pasic's family and others, the incident I described at the beginning of this opening. We can see that the commanders in the 1st Krajina Corps fully appreciated the crime that was perpetrated there: "Massacre of the captured members of the Green Berets started because of the wounding of four and killing of one soldier ... and the burning of the wounded soldiers ... measures to prevent further massacres were taken ... with the exception of Kotor Varos, where we have taken serious intentions to prevent a genocide of Muslims. Women and children from the area have been allowed to pass through Travnik." The third objective was to establish a corridor of Serb-held lands in Eastern Bosnia. The third objective envisaged that this land would become Serb controlled and populated with Serbs. The indictment charges a representative group of crimes committed in seven municipalities, including Mladic's hometown of Kalinovik. Let me call once again to the screen the demographic map from 1991. You can see the area falling within the third objective in the circle on the right. Here we can see that it is predominantly green, indicating Muslim majorities. By the time Mladic was appointed the commander of the Main Staff on the 12th of May, most of the municipalities within the third objective were under Serb control. His intention was turned fully to ethnically cleansing the area. In November 1992, Mladic would sign directive number 4, ordering the VRS to force that part of the population in Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas that were Muslim to leave: "The Drina Corps: From its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad (the dam), Zvornik and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region are to exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on them and force them with the Muslim population to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas." As can be seen in this directive, the Muslim population is directly made a target of military operations. What you see before you on slide 59 is an order from the 28th of May, 1992, issued by the commander of the Birac Brigade. It refers to the area around Zvornik, Bratunac, and Vlasenica. The order makes clear that the expulsion of the predominantly Muslim population who lived and worked in Eastern Bosnia was to be organised and co-ordinated. Women and children would be moved out, the men placed in detention centres for exchange: "The moving out of the Muslim population must be organised and co-ordinated ... only women and children can move out, while men fit for military service are to be placed in camps for exchange." On the 2nd of June, Bosnian Serb forces, supported by armoured personnel carriers and machine-guns, attacked the small hamlet of Drum in Vlasenica. Soldiers went from house to house, killing every man they could find. They found about 20. All of them but one was shot in the forehead. On the 6th of July, 1992, non-Serbs from Mladic's hometown of Kalinovik were moved from a school to an ammunition depot in the village of Jelasako Polje. VRS soldiers guarded them. After a month around the 5th of August, the men were loaded onto trucks after having had their hands bound with wire. They were driven to an open field and killed. Approximately 20 men died. Slide 60 is an excerpt of the evidence of Fejzija Hadzic. Fejzija pretended to be dead after being shot in the leg. "Now the remaining Muslim ... was ordered to pour accelerant over the bodies and set them alight. He refused to set light to us. He was pleading with them to spare his life. The sound of his voice will stick in my mind forever. They just shot him dead and he was added to the pile of bodies." On the 22nd of September, 1992, the VRS 2nd Romanija Brigade surrounded the town of Novoseoci. There was no armed resistance. After Bosnian Serb soldiers had full control of the town, one of them read an order that the women and children were to be placed on buses and moved out of the area. The men were told that they would remain and would do forced labour. After the women and children were taken away, all of the men were murdered. The realisation of the third strategic objective was almost complete in 1992. The large population centres of Muslims had been largely emptied. Slide 61 shows an entry from Mladic's military notebook. In it we can see him noting a report about how the project of ethnic cleansing has progressed in Foca. Here Miroslav Stanic of the Foca War Presidency informs him that the ethnic make-up of Foca has changed from 49 per cent Serb before the war to 99 per cent as of the 17th of September, 1992, over 20.000 Muslims removed from the municipality. Crimes of sexual violence for an integral part of the process of taking over and ethnically cleansing Bosnia. While women were most often targeted for such crimes of terrible violation, men were also victimised. Sometimes the perpetrators sexually assaulted the victims. On other occasions the perpetrators forced the victims to perform sexual acts on others, including relatives. The indictment against Mladic charges crimes of sexual violence, focusing on the crimes of sexual violence perpetrated in Foca where the systematic rapes of women were commonplace. Slide 62 includes an excerpt from the testimony of RM070, evidence the Prosecution will seek to tender in this case: "I didn't even look to see who had come or who had left the room. The world should see, to look in our eyes ... "They had killed my mother before that, they had killed my brother. And up to that day I had been raped by almost 50 of them ... "I didn't want to see who was coming in, who was going out ... "And whenever they would bring me back ... I would just tear my hair and say, 'Oh, what are they doing to us?'" The Prosecution will tender evidence establishing the many crimes of systematic sexual violence perpetrated against women in places like Karaman's house in Foca, Foca high school, and the Partizan hall. Here on slide 63, Mladic records a report from Ljubisav Simic from Bratunac that a 64 per cent Muslim population in Bratunac has been reduced to two individual Muslims: "In Bratunac municipality we now have two Muslims." As the scourge of ethnic cleansing continued and took full effect in Eastern Bosnia, those ethnically cleansed gathered in the three eastern enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. The success of the third strategic objective was left unfulfilled by 1993. The VRS's move towards the town of Srebrenica was halted by the intervention of UNPROFOR in 1993. General Morillon would make his well-known promise to the people of Srebrenica, and in the years of 1993 to 1995 the eastern enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde survived under UN protection. Here on slide 64, we can see an entry from Mladic's military notebook recording Morillon's admonition to resist any urge he may have to ethnically cleanse these areas. The situation in Eastern Bosnia largely remained for two years. During this period Muslim fighters from the enclaves raided surrounding Serb communities, on some occasions committing terrible war crimes themselves. The situation remained volatile during the months leading up to July 1995. The people in the eastern enclaves would remain under threat until the time Mladic would order the take-over of Srebrenica and Zepa. Slide 65 is an excerpt from the evidence of David Harland, a senior UN official. It recounts the situation in which Mladic threatened to kill everyone in the eastern enclaves unless 22 VRS prisoners of war were returned to him. As Harland points out, such threats were not uncommon for Mladic. I will not spend time on the implementation of the fourth and sixth strategic objectives. Although crimes were also committed in furtherance of these goals, the indictment does not contain any specific crimes arising from them. I will now turn to the fifth strategic objective, the division of Sarajevo. Before the war, Sarajevo was emblematic of the Yugoslav ideal: 500.000 people of all ethnicities living together, working side by side, raising their children together, celebrating each other's happy occasions. The compact geography of the city circled a true inter-ethnic community, prosperous and peaceful. Marriage across ethnic lines was not uncommon, and though many identified themselves as Yugoslavs, others proudly and rightly identified themselves by their ethnic affiliation. Beginning in 1991 and continuing into early 1992, the ethnic delineation of Sarajevo's neighbourhoods and areas was a focus of SDS political activity. From December 1991, SDS organs in Sarajevo's greater urban area, territories including Pale, Ilijas, Ilidza, and Novi Grad moved to unilaterally proclaim areas of existing municipalities as Serb. Tensions increased in the city during the spring of 1992. Barricades would be erected in early March, affecting the freedom of movement around the city. The barricades provoked a popular response with thousand of protesters marching to demand their removal. Peace demonstrations took place intermittently over the next month, while Serb forces used the time to expand their control over institutions and areas around the city. On the 4th of April, the police school in Vrace, a high point south of Sarajevo's main thoroughfare was taken over. On 6th of April, Sarajevans of all ethnicities responded to the rising tension with a peaceful march in the centre of the city. The crowd dispersed when gunmen shot into the crowd from the Holiday Inn. Between the 4th of April and mid-May 1992, the contours of Sarajevo's encirclement were established. The physical separation of Sarajevo's population along ethnic lines was well underway. The city was effectively dissected. Elements of a campaign of terror, the sniping and indiscriminate shelling of Sarajevo's citizens was already a feature of their daily life. From April through May, Serb forces fought units fighting in the name of the Bosnian government, containing them in what would eventually be known as the "inner ring" around the city. Shelling and sniping of Sarajevo's central areas from the Serb-controlled hills had begun in a campaign that was to last until 1995. On the 6th of June, Mladic and Karadzic both would meet with SDS representatives from Serb-claimed Sarajevo municipalities. That same day Mladic issued the first of his military directives to the VRS, directive number 1. It called for the cleansing of those parts of Sarajevo with a majority Serb population and cutting it along an axis defined by Bosnian Serb leaders. It included an order for the military implementation of the first and fifth strategic goals in the Sarajevo area. While Serb leaders held on to the notion of ethnic division as a primary principle of their vision for Sarajevo, they quickly realised that their stranglehold on the city offered an opportunity for an important strategic advantage. Every successive military directive called for the continued blockade of the city. The actual Siege of Sarajevo advanced purposes separate and apart from the strategic objectives. In short, Sarajevo, the location of the newly established government of an independent Bosnia, was a pressure point, the place where Bosnian Serbs could exert pressure in an effort to influence negotiations or punish the Bosnian civilians for something that had occurred elsewhere in the country. At the 16th Assembly Session in May 1992, Mladic described the encirclement of the city with artillery and snipers as a ring around its neck. He was acutely aware that he held the power to decide who entered and left the city and exploited this power throughout the siege. I'm going to ask you to take a look at your screens and I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to play a media report by a former Sky news correspondent by the name of Aernout van Lynden in which Mladic talks about Sarajevo. After the video concludes, I will pause for a considerable period of time to make -- be sure that the video has been fully translated into each of our languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "He is the scourge of Sarajevo. The chief warrior of the Serbs. He is called Ratko Mladic, appropriately, Ratko means warrior and this square jawed Serb general has lived up to the name. The commander always on the move, the visit to one of the mountain's chalets where the Serbs of Bosnia have established their separatist government is but a fleeting one. In a short briefing, the Commander-in-Chief speaks only of attacks on his forces, never of offences by them. And as if to prove the point, he gives us a rare chance to accompany him to front line artillery positions where the UN observers are conspicuous by their absence. High up on the wind swept hills the 100-millimetre guns are dug deep in the rocks directly overlooking Sarajevo. An overwhelming position of strength which is obviously to the general's satisfaction. As he says, he holds the city in his palm and many of the buildings in the haze below, they are testimony to that power. Yet General Mladic is quite unrepentant. He is a man who has no doubts, only a total assurance that he is right, the world wrong, and that his people have been slandered. "I hope the UN Security Council first takes measures to understand that we Serbs are a reality in this world not some sort of extraterrestrials and that we have the right to defend ourselves. "Nearby more positions are being dug. In general's eyes the world may deny his people their rights but that's not going to stop him. "We have to fight as long as we continue to exist to defend ourselves. There is no other way and we are prepared for a long war. "Far away from the battle-field, the UN is preparing a resolution on war crimes. It leaves Ratko Mladic quite unmoved. "I am not bothered at all. I did not take part in any crimes. I have only defended my people. "With that, the general departs to inspect other front lines in a war neither he not his officers believe will end any time soon. Aernout van Lynden, Sky news, on the front lines outside Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mladic would demonstrate his power over Sarajevo two weeks after he became commander of the Main Staff. Throughout May there were contentious negotiations over the evacuation of the JNA barracks in Sarajevo. Skirmishes had taken place. After assuming command of the Main Staff in mid-May, Mladic threatened to retaliate against the city if any of the JNA personnel were attacked. He did just that. The following intercept concerns the shelling of Bascarsija, an area in the old town of Sarajevo. Mladic exacted his campaign of terror among civilians shell after shell after shell, not aimed at identifiable military targets, but scattered across the city in bombardments designed to cause panic and terror. There was no safety in knowing you are in a purely residential, civilian neighbourhood. In the intercept I will ask Ms. Stewart to now play, you will hear Mladic directing artillery fire at the densely populated Bascarsija area in the old town. I would ask for you to listen to it now. The translation of what Mladic says can be found on slide 69.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "How soon could you fire? "Well, I could fire in five to ten minutes, no sooner than that. "Tell me, can you also shell Bascarsija? "Yes, I can. "I beg your pardon? "I can, I can. "Fire a salvo at Bascarsija as well. "Yes, sir!"

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Immediately after this bombardment Mladic would record General John Wilson from the Senior Military Liaison Officer to the UN mission conveying a personal appeal to Mladic from the then-Secretary-General, Boutros Boutros-Ghali. Mladic's notes are displayed in slide 70. The Secretary-General expressed his concern at the destruction of the city. A week later in furtherance of his first military directive, Mladic would unleash another ferocious barrage of artillery fire against the city. From the start it was clear to the victims, to the perpetrators, to the world community watching on their televisions that the bombardment of the civilians of Sarajevo was a grave criminal act. Slobodan Milosevic himself would acknowledge what was obvious to all. In this UN cable written by General Nambiar, he reports Milosevic as describing these initiate bombardments of Sarajevo as "bloody criminal." To appreciate the Siege of Sarajevo, to understand how it was conducted and why it caused such terror to Sarajevans, one must understand the city's topography. Sarajevo was situated on a deep valley on the Miljacka River surrounded by hills to the north, east, and south. For the most part, Sarajevo was densely populated, a mixture of high-rise apartment blocks and compact residential two- to three-storey houses on small plots of land, all within sight of the hills rising around the city. From any roof-top or high-rise window, Sarajevans could see Serb territory close by, in some areas no more than a block away. Sarajevans lived with a sense of vulnerability that came with knowing every part of the city was within the range of Serb weaponry. Running down the main arteries of the city was its life-line, the tram line. Until May 1992, Sarajevans from Ilidza to the old town centre would come to the tram line to take it to work, to shop along its streets, to school, to the old town for a coffee with friends on the weekend. The tram was used each day by many, many Sarajevans. As Mladic himself said in May of 1992: "I have blocked Sarajevo from all four sides. There is no exit. It is in a mousetrap." To give you a sense of the proximity of the hills surrounding Sarajevo and the vulnerability of the entire city to artillery fire, I ask that you look at a short clip of video taken from the turret of an artillery position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: From 1992 until 1996, the Bosnian Serb goals in Sarajevo were to divide it and to use terror to exert pressure on the Bosnian leadership. The mechanisms of terror were simple: Indiscriminate shelling, sniping of civilians, deprivation of the essentials of daily life, food, water, and humanitarian aid. As David Harland, a senior UN official has testified, Sarajevo was a "spigot of terror," one to be turned on and off as needed. Please remember this image. It is an apt characterisation of what Sarajevo was to Mladic and other Bosnian Serb leaders: "Sarajevo, ... in the context of ... political objectives, that is, of getting the Muslims to negotiate, or in terms of deterring any NATO military attack on them. Our sense was they - there was, as it were, a spigot of terror which they would open or close according to how much pressure was on them from the international community or what political concessions they hoped to get from the other side." Your Honours, to give you a sense of what it was like to live in Sarajevo during the siege, we have created a compilation of news reports spanning the period of the indictment. The entire video is approximately four minutes long and will give you a sense of what happened when this spigot of terror was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Dusk in Sarajevo. Amongst the city's ancient minarets the rockets fall heralding another night of heavy shelling. "In Sarajevo, the crossroads can be lethal, need to be taken at speed. They and the avenues that cut across the city offer the Serb gunners in the hills above with open lines of fire. Flying targets which the old and the infirm are forced to accept as the new uncomfortable realities of life. "Sarajevo's burning, in its heart and in its suburbs. "Zijad Kojundzic is alive because he decided to listen to the 4.00 news last Friday afternoon. He left his family sheltering in the cellar and with his son Muris went upstairs. While the news was on, the house was hit by a tank round. This morning, Mr. Kojundzic buried his wife, his daughter, two of his grandchildren and a friend who had come around to their house with some aspirin. The graveyard was shelled while they were there. There isn't a time or a place where the citizens of Sarajevo can feel safe. Some parts of the city are more dangerous than others, but the shelling is indiscriminate and it kills people every day. "The lives of the people of Sarajevo get more difficult all the time. At least half the city is without water. A tap in a burnt-out kiosk near the ruins of the railway station has shorter queues than most because it is overlooked by a sniper. Guns fired with intent to kill are so much a part of the daily routine here that they hardly notice. "Even by the crazed standards of Sarajevo, a horrendous night. Each luminous blob deadly and indiscriminate. Deafening and relentless, artillery and mortar fire speckled with machine-guns and rifle bullets. In the dark places below are over 300.000 citizens enduring a Serbian onslaught, possibly in retaliation for an attempt by the Bosnians to break out from the siege in the past few days. "This is supposed to be a safe area in the making. There was supposed to be a cease-fire, but the shelling has been getting worse for the last 48 hours and today the people of Sarajevo suffered as much as on any day in this war. "When the war was starting, sniping like this would have sent them to their cellars. These days it's different. They know how to take cover, when to wait, and when to run. It's still terrifying and deadly, but like fetching water it's part of the daily grind. "In Sarajevo the horrors are not just heard of but lived through day by day. This is a particularly heavy bombardment of the old city. A single artillery shell fell on a queue of people waiting to pick up water outside the brewery. Eight were killed, 18 seriously injured. Of the dead, three came from one family - the mother and father who were killed instantly and the daughter ... "The UN commander is dispensing calm assurance, but it wasn't being felt at street level just afterwards where people were fleeing from yet another sniper attack. We asked one of them how long it had been going on. 'Two and a half years,' he said. "The efforts to cling to a kind of normality in Sarajevo are being undermined. Not yet driven underground and into shelters, much of the population is at risk. As this morning a shell landing among people walking near the Holiday Inn. With only the occasional random lethal explosion, people are still walking to work, queuing for food or tending their allotments. Taking a chance. But this morning five were injured, two seriously. And there has been sniper fire around the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I've already discussed directive 1, which relates in part to Sarajevo. Other VRS military directives also apply to Sarajevo. These directives contained instructions for the military activities of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Slide 75 depicts two directives. Directive 3 was issued in August of 1992 and signed by Mladic. A portion of that directive is dedicated to the operational objectives of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of the VRS or the SRK. Every directive that was issued instructed the SRK to maintain the blockade of Sarajevo: "Keep Sarajevo firmly under blockade and prevent its breaking." Directive 6, issued and signed by Karadzic as supreme commander, was promulgated in November 1993. It also contains instructions for the SRK, including the instruction to: "Use the main body of forces to prevent the deblockade of Sarajevo." Throughout the course of the 44-month siege, the blockade of Sarajevo was unbroken. The city remained in the palm of Mladic's hand. The Prosecution will meet its burden on the shelling component of the Siege of Sarajevo in two ways: First, through evidence of Sarajevans and international observers, who will describe significant periods of intense shelling of the city, shelling that for the most part had no identifiable military purpose and in fact was clearly directed at terrorising civilians; second, the Prosecution will meet its burden by leading evidence of a number of specific shelling crimes which are representative of the shelling campaign. I have already described three of the shelling crimes for you. The last shelling incident I will deal with in this opening is one in which a modified air bomb was used. These large, heavy, destructive bombs were designed to be dropped from planes, gravity taking them to their targets. With the imposition of a no-fly zone in October of 1992, such bombs could no longer be used with planes. Steps were taken to modify these bombs so that they could be launched from the hills overlooking Sarajevo. Powerful rocket motors were affixed so that they could be launched from purpose-built launching ramps. Without any mechanism to aim or steer them, these bombs were simply rocketed up into the sky above Sarajevo to fall haphazardly on the city below. These weapons were developed by the Yugoslav army, and Mladic was directly involved in procuring them for use in and around Sarajevo. These large bombs were capable of causing great destruction and were notoriously inaccurate. The victims of modified air bombs were not only those living where they fell, but all those who knew such indiscriminate weapons were being regularly used by the VRS. The Prosecution will lead detailed evidence of three air bomb attacks in the spring of 1995. I will focus on just one. It is briefly described in Schedule G10 of the indictment. On the 7th of April, 1995, a modified air bomb was launched from a VRS launcher and fell onto a residential area in Hrasnica at the foot of Mount Igman. Slide 76 is an order from SRK corps commander, Dragomir Milosevic. Here on the 6th of April, 1995, he issued the following order: "The Ilidza Brigade will immediately prepare a launcher with an aerial bomb and transport the bomb for launching. The most profitable target must be selected in Hrasnica and Sokolovici colony where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted." Slide 77, a report sent to the Main Staff the next day, shows that the order was carried out: "In Ilidza Brigade one 120-millimetre shell was fired and one 250-kilogramme aerial bomb was launched at the centre of Hrasnica." This particular bomb destroyed civilians houses, killed one civilian and wounded three others. Ziba Custovic was home drinking her morning coffee when the bomb killed her. Prosecution evidence will establish that the use of heavy weapons was controlled through an established, centralised military hierarchy. The following is an example of the type of document the Prosecution will tender to establish this. Here on slide 78 we can see an order from the Main Staff to the SRK command. The Main Staff retained to itself the authorisation to use heavy weapons, authority which it might delegate to the corps level but no further down the military hierarchy. "VRS Main Staff decides on the use of aerial bombs and possibly a corps if the VRS Main Staff approves so and not a brigade according to its own plan ... in future, they cannot directly address without your approval ..." Later that year on the 7th of November, 1994, Mladic himself would issue an order reserving to himself the decision to use heavy-calibre weapons on civilian targets in Sarajevo. In this order we can see Mladic's direct involvement when it related to civilian targets. He says here in paragraph 3: "I forbid all use of weapons of bigger calibre on civilian targets in Sarajevo without my approval." There can be no doubt that Mladic, subject to Karadzic's authority, controlled the shelling of Sarajevo. As Mladic says to John Wilson, he was going to make Sarajevo shake: "Make sure that your soldiers are aware that Sarajevo is going to shake ... Sarajevo will shake, more shells will fall on per second than in the entire war so far." The command structure of the VRS was well developed and operated efficiently. Mladic was able to use it quickly to stop any shelling or sniping activities that may have been in progress. This ability was demonstrated during the cease-fires when Karadzic and Mladic were able to deliver a cease-fire that had been reached in peace negotiations. Slide 81 is a report from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. It reports that the Main Staff of the VRS has issued a warning for troops not to take any action over Sarajevo because Karadzic has entered into a cease-fire agreement: "We received from the command of the Main Staff of VRS a warning not to act over proper Sarajevo. Act only in the case of necessary self-defence and endangering military defence lines. The warning is issued with regard to the agreement between President Karadzic, UNPROFOR, and our enemy." Command structures were in place for Karadzic and Mladic to start, stop, or modulate the shelling and sniping activity towards Sarajevo. The spigot, to use David Harland's phrase, worked well. Your Honours, I'm about to move to the topic of sniping. May I inquire about the time the Chamber plans to take the next break so I can break accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I had on my mind to have the next break at -- in approximately five minutes, but if it would be more suitable to take it now then there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break and we'll resume at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm now going to talk about sniping. Sniping played a different role in the campaign of terror against Sarajevans. The noisy imprecision of the modified air bombs was in contrast to the lethal silence of the sniper's bullet. Sarajevans would hide behind buildings and shipping containers, gathering the courage to dash across a street where others had felled before. In silent perches around the city, VRS soldiers waited in vantage points above the tram line, above paths civilians had to travel to get food, water, fuel for heat, waiting silently, finger poised on the trigger until someone dared to rush in front of the cross-hairs of a scope. The main street running along the Miljacka River became so famous for the number of shootings that it was called Sniper's Alley. One of these snipers will appear before you and provide evidence of this aspect of the campaign of terror. He will describe his orders to shoot at anything that moved down below his perch. Other witnesses will provide evidence of how snipers were trained and how the activity of snipers around the city was co-ordinated. Today Nermin Divovic would be 25. Back on the 18th of November, 1994, he was 7, growing up in a Sarajevo under siege. Nermin was returning with his mother and sister from collecting firewood. As they crossed a street on their way home, a sniper aligned his rifle towards Nermin's mother. His bullet passed through her abdomen and struck Nermin, who had been walking beside her. The sniper's bullet struck his head causing a catastrophic and mortal injury. The little boy dropped dead onto the pavement below his mother's feet. She thought he was simply doing what she had taught him to do, lie down when you hear gun-fire: "I was at the first crossing. My girl crossed - ran across and I stayed behind with Nermin, and I just saw that my boy fell down, and because I would always tell him, Son, when there's shooting, lie down, and I didn't realise that he was wounded until UNPROFOR put him behind the bushes. At that moment I wasn't aware my little boy was killed." Slide 83 is a picture from a sniper's nest. Over the course of the case the Prosecution will tender photos from a number of snipers' nests. What these and other pictures will make clear is that sniping in Sarajevo was often from close distances, sometimes a matter of a few hundred metres. Mladic's use of snipers in the context of the attack on the civilian population was not at all like the use of snipers in armed conflict. It was a strategy of shooting civilians from a hiding spot, giving them no warning or reasonable prospect of taking cover. It was about creating insecurity, about creating terror. Here is a photo from another sniper's nest. The photographer did not use any magnification in taking the picture and took the photo to depict the edges of the hole where the barrel went through. You can get some sense of the scale and the proximity of the tram there just below the sniper's nest. The Prosecution will also tender documentary evidence regarding sniping. Here in slide 85 an intelligence officer from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of the VRS states: "Sniping is to be stopped only by orders and the inner organisation and accordingly by taking of adequate measures." It specifically notes that the final decision on any measures related to sniping would be taken by the corps commander. John Jordan was a volunteer fireman for the US who travelled to Sarajevo to help fellow firefighters after seeing them being sniped as they tried to put out fires, to assist people who had been injured. He made the following observations: "What excuse can there be for shooting a firefighter while he's trying to put out a residential fire? What reason can there be for shelling water lines, bread lines, places with no military purpose? I can't remember a time when we weren't picking up wounded and dead people. The thing I noticed about certain attacks was that Serb shooters would often go after the youngest in the family ... in a crowd of girls, it seemed that the most attractive would be shot. It seemed that there was something very personal, almost grudge attacks, doing whatever would cause the most pain to the survivors." On the 15th of August, 1994, Ratko Mladic spent part of the day driving Milan Lesic, a supporter from Canada, around Eastern Bosnia. Lesic's video recorded some of their travels and his conversation with Mladic. They are driving down a road that reminded Mladic that his men had once cleared that road of barricades using chain-saws and tanks. Mladic turns the conversation to Sarajevo and how sniper fire disrupted the traffic there. Slide 87 is a still from that video showing Mladic as he drives the car. He says: "And whenever I come by Sarajevo, I kill someone in passing. That's why the traffic for Sarajevo was disrupted ... snipers. I go, kick the hell out of the Turks." This statement was captured on the video recording. The camera is pointing out of the car or at his dashboard, but it is what Mr. Mladic says that we are most interested in. I will ask Ms. Stewart to play the video now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Now I will drive you as if you were a director. "On this road? "On this road, but I fucked them. I led them there, made a mask, and then we cleaned up the barricades here with chain-saws, this all had been blocked. And then we brought tanks here and kicked the hell out of the Turks. "Kicked the hell out of them? "And whenever I come by Sarajevo, I kill someone in passing. That's why the traffic for Sarajevo was disrupted. I go kick the hell out of the Turks, who gives a fuck for them! Somehow I and my have to ... I don't know whether you kill that kind over there in Canada and America, you ought to kill these Ustashas there and those who support them and ours as well as those who collaborate those with them. "Yes, those should be first."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mladic talks about personally sniping the people of Sarajevo as if it were a sport, a form of recreation. For the many injured, killed, for the thousands who crossed the street each day, sent their children to school not knowing if the day would end in tragedy, it was not recreation. The combined effect of indiscriminate shelling and the sniping of civilians was a persistent fog of terror that permeated the lives of all who lived through it. During the siege between April 1992 until November 1995, those who lived in Sarajevo lived with the ever-present reality that serious injury or death awaited them each minute, each time they stepped out from a building, each time they put their children to bed. Walking wasn't safe, driving wasn't safe, the tram wasn't safe, your home wasn't safe. This terror designed by Karadzic and Mladic and visited upon Sarajevo was the grim reality for Sarajevans during the siege. The first strategic objective, ethnic separation. The first and most important strategic objective was its demographic one: Ethnic separation, ensuring that the lands controlled by Bosnian Serbs were devoid of Muslims and Croats. Slide 90 is a document from the 1st Krajina Corps less than ten days after the formation of the VRS. "... Serbian people ... must struggle for complete separation from the Muslim and Croatian peoples and form their own state." The Bosnian Serb army Main Staff co-ordinated the removal of people ethnically cleansed from their homes. Slide 91 shows a report from the Drina Corps to the VRS Main Staff. On the 31st of January, 1993, here the Zvornik Brigade opened a corridor for ten hours so that those ethnically cleansed from their homes in Eastern Bosnia could leave the area. Slide 92 is a UN report from October 1992. It demonstrates that the clear pattern of killing, rape, and destruction of homes made clear that ethnic cleansing was the purpose of military action and not the unintended consequence: "Ethnic cleansing does not appear to be the consequence of the war but rather its goal. This goal, to a large extent, has already been achieved through killings, beatings, rape, destruction of houses and threats ... hundreds of thousands of people being forced to leave their homes and to abandon their belongings in order to save their lives." Here in slide 93 Mladic is told that people were being evicted. There can be no question of people fleeing war. This is the forcible removal of people from their homes. Mladic notes: "We were most active in evicting the Muslims, we had brought peace to Sepak, Divic, and Kozluk. Some of them wanted to move out, and we also demanded it." Kozluk was a town north of Zvornik. The Muslim population had turned over all weapons and agreed to recognise the new Serb authorities. This entry is a reference to the day buses arrived and every single person in Kozluk was made to board the bus. They were transported through Serbia to the Hungarian border. Earlier I showed you an entry from Mladic's notebook regarding the progress of ethnic cleansing in Bratunac. Here on slide 94 is another entry regarding Bratunac in which Mladic notes that there are no Muslims in Bratunac, the town is considered fully liberated. Another way Bosnian Serb leaders sought to make ethnic cleansing permanent was the destruction of religious and cultural property. In some cases churches and mosques were destroyed and in some cases the land was paved for parking-lots, or other buildings were erected on the site. The Prosecution will limit its evidence regarding the destruction of religious and cultural property to the destruction in 11 municipalities. But even from this limited presentation, the Chamber will be able to conclude that such destruction was part of a campaign of persecution. One of the most important tools for ethnic cleansing was the co-ordinated system of gathering non-Serbs, concentrating them in detention centres, and ultimately ejecting them from Bosnian Serb-held territory. Bosnian Serb leaders established a system of ejecting non-Serbs under the misnomer of exchanges. From the outset this system was created to include the detention and forcible removal of civilians from targeted territory. On the 8th of May, 1992, a central commission for the exchange of prisoners was established and immediately began the process of organising the collection of prisoners, both military and civilian, and in ensuring, at least in the case of civilian detainees, that they were removed to areas that were not targeted by Serbs. Slide 95 shows a document from the Bosnian Serb police dated the 2nd of July, 1992. The document makes clear two things: First, that in the overall enterprise the Bosnian Serb army is to play a prominent role in the capture of as many Muslim civilians as possible; and second, that the detention camps that these people are to be placed in, these camps do not observe international norms: "The army, Crisis Staffs, and War Presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible and they leave such undefined camps to internal affairs organs. The conditions in some of these camps are poor: There is no food, individuals sometimes do not observe international norms, et cetera." Bosnian Serb leaders created a co-ordinated system through which non-Serbs could be gathered, counted them, prevented them from resettling in Serb-conquered areas, and either killed them or permanently ejected them. Slide 96 illustrates the role these detention facilities played in ethnic cleansing. This slide refers to the detention facility known as Kula. It is described in indictment Schedule C8.1. Here a member of the of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on the 17th of June, 1992, is expressing concern that the camp is being used to separate civilians according to their ethnicity. You will see that such cautions were ignored and the crimes in Kula went on for about two and a half years after this report was filed. Each municipality had its own local system for detaining non-Serbs. Impromptu detention centres were set up in police stations, local schools, factories, garages, as needed; places like Karaman's house in Foca or the elementary school in Kalinovik. Here detainees were brutalised, tortured, and many detainees were killed. Soon larger facilities were established. These facilities served as regional detention facilities and received prisoners from municipal authorities, facilities such as Batkovic, Kula. The most notorious of these camps, Omarska and Keraterm in Prijedor were run by Republika Srpska police officers with VRS personnel providing security around the perimeter. The VRS also directly established some camps. Manjaca camp in Banja Luka, Batkovic camp near Bijeljina were both established by the VRS. Susica camp in Vlasenica was established by an order signed by a Mayor Andric. Here on slide 97 we can see the actual order by Mladic relating to the establishment of Manjaca camp. You will hear from Osman Selak, a former colonel in the Yugoslav Army, who was present on the 1st of June, 1992, when Colonel Momir Talic issued the order to establish Manjaca. Talic's order to establish Manjaca on the 1st of June was formalised by this order issued on the 12th of June. I will pause for a moment to allow you to read it. Dr. Enes Sabanovic will describe the routine physical abuse and inhumane conditions at Manjaca. As a doctor detained in the camp, he was forced to falsify death certificates, covering up the murders of inmates. Your Honours, I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to play a video from a news report on Manjaca camp. Although the reporter speaks English, the sound has deteriorated over the years. We have added English subtitles to assist you in understanding what the reporter is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Shed which in better days might have housed animals now it homes more than 600 men. Here, the prisoners live, eat and sleep 24 hours a day. Most of these men just arrived three days ago from the camp at Omarska. Their faces still haunted by memories they did not dare relate in the presence of their guards. Conditions here, they told him, things are much better than the place they had just come from. "The Serb leadership is under tremendous pressure to allow outsiders access to these camps. The proposed UN resolution would authorise any means necessary to implement that access as well as guarantee the supply of humanitarian aid ... prisoners we asked maintain they were civilians not soldiers. Those we saw were crammed into cattle sheds where they expend all day and all night huddled together like ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There can be no doubt that Mladic and his subordinates who ran some of these camps or participated in the operation of others were fully aware of what was taking place there. In this report on slide 99, we can see that the officials in Manjaca fully appreciated the illegality of these facilities and the role they played in ethnic cleansing: "This camp can be considered as a detention camp, that is, a camp for the segregation of Muslims and Croats which history will not forgive us." In fact, in many cases detaining these prisoners served a dual purpose for the Bosnian Serb leaders. In addition to facilitating the ethnic cleansing, these detention camps in some instances gathered people to be used as hostages. As Zupljanin noted in slide 100: "The third category is composed of adult men about whom the service does not have any information of security interest for us so far. Therefore, they can be used as hostages." All of these camps were part of a system for the detention and mistreatment of non-Serbs targeted in the ethnic cleansing campaign. The camps were integral to the overall project of taking land from non-Serbs who lived there. These detention camps were places of great suffering. Food was insufficient, sanitation was often rudimentary and inadequate, insufficient for the large number of prisoners. Detainees were often the subject of regular beatings, torture, rape, and other crimes of sexual violence and murder. The conditions were inhumane. They would have been insufficient to sustain farm animals, let alone humans. In addition to the inhumane conditions, prisoners were regularly beaten, sometimes so extreme as to result in death. I would now like to play a video depicting men detained at Trnopolje. There is some inaudible speech in the video. There is no translation and the Prosecution is relying only on the images and not on what the prisoners are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In one night alone in July 1992 at the Keraterm camp in Prijedor, approximately 150 men were murdered. That same month about 150 men were killed at Omarska. Approximately 140 Susica prisoners were killed on a single occasion in September 1992. Survivors of these camps will describe conditions in those camps that are simply beyond the realm of our experience. An excerpt of the evidence of RM008 is now on the screen in slide 102. He was a witness to the massacre of 150 men in Keraterm in what is referred to as the Room 3 massacre: "Q. Do you know how many people were eventually detained in Room no. 3 at Keraterm? "A. Once when they were counted, it was 570. People were packed like sardines. And there was... perspiration. There was condensation on the walls, so it was very hot and people licked those walls to get something because there was no water." None of us can imagine conditions so harsh, none of us can imagine a thirst so vicious that it would drive someone to lick condensed sweat off a wall. I would like to conclude my remarks on the detention camps by showing you a map of the major camps in the indictment. Slide 103 indicates the location of the major detention centres in which the people taken prisoner in the municipalities and first kept at smaller detention sites were sent. As you can see in the area of the second strategic objective, there are Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Manjaca. In the area of the third strategic objective, there are Batkovic, Vlasenica, Rasadnik, and KP Dom. Kula was outside Sarajevo. This was an integrated system of detention and mistreatment specifically designed to help realise the strategic objectives. Consider the case of RM041 who had the misfortune of being held in six different facilities. His path has been traced on slide 103. He began in the local Veljko Vlahovic school detention centre in Rogatica and then was transferred to Rasadnik, then to the police station in Zvornik, on to Batkovic, back to Rasadnik, and finally on to Kula, from which he was ultimately released. Other witnesses will describe their journey through the camp system, moving through several of the large camps in the Krajina and ultimately escaping or being released alive if they were fortunate. The prisoners in these camps were used as a source of forced labour, in some cases being forced to engage in work in dangerous battle zones. Some of the transfers between camps was done to meet labour needs. During the trial, the Prosecution will tender military documents setting out in greater detail this system. The hostage crisis. The last component of the Prosecution case arises from the hostage crisis in 1995, an incident in which UN peacekeepers were taken hostage by members of the VRS. On the 31st of August, 1994, the German weekly "Der Spiegel" published an interview with Radovan Karadzic. You can see an excerpt from it on slide 104 -- I'm sorry, 105, if we could advance to that slide. In that interview he was explicit about his intention to order the taking of hostages and in particular UN personnel referred to in the article as "blue helmets." Karadzic, acting together with Mladic, went through with this threat and it is the subject of Count 11 of the indictment, the war crime of taking hostages. I would like to return to Sarajevo in order to provide you some background on the hostage crisis, that period between the 26th of May and the 19th of June, 1995, when Mladic's forces took over 200 UN peacekeepers hostage. The 16th of May, 1995, the VRS commenced some of its heaviest shelling of Sarajevo, certainly since 1993. In May 1995, there were seven teams of UN military observers stationed across the city. Their job was to monitor military activity. This entailed, in part, counting the shells fired into Sarajevo. On this day, 17 years ago, in response to a Bosnian army mortar attack on the VRS Lukavica barracks, over 1.500 detonations were recorded in Sarajevo. Over 1.500 shells sent into the city by the Bosnian Serb army. On the 24th of May General Rupert Smith, the UNPROFOR commander, gave Karadzic and Mladic an ultimatum to cease the heavy weapons bombardment. They refused to comply and in response NATO planes attacked two Bosnian Serb ammunition depots. The VRS responded by preventing some UN military observers from leaving their posts and by removing others and detaining them at different locations. The VRS abducted 33 more UN personnel from observation posts around Gorazde. In Sarajevo dozens of UNPROFOR members were taken hostage between the 26th and 27th of May. Here on slide 106 a peacekeeper describes the matter-of-fact way in which he was taken hostage: "The officer, in a very decisive tone, said that from then on he was in charge that we -- he said exactly that, from that very moment, we were being taken hostage by the army." The VRS also used UN hostages and their uniforms to raid and take control of additional UN observation posts and to capture additional hostages. By the end of May over 200 UN personnel were in the VRS custody with at least 17 of them being used as human shields to protect VRS installations from further air-strikes. One such UNMO was filmed by local television tied to a radar station. When he was brought to the site he overheard some of his captors say that Mladic wanted UN personnel to be filmed at the radar site. The UN personnel were held by force or by the threat of force. Most were kept incommunicado from their superior command. Some were beaten, physically mistreated, or threatened. On the 26th of May, Mr. Mladic spoke with General Nikolaj and General Rupert Smith. On slide number 107 you can see an excerpt from this conversation. In this particular portion of the conversation, Mladic acknowledges that UNPROFOR personnel have been placed at installations that were targeted in NATO air-strikes: "I have been informed that you are holding in detention eight of my unarmed UN observers, and also that three of them are tied to an ammunition fence in Pale. And also that by your order these men will be killed in case there will be new air-strikes ... "Mladic: I have been informed that some UNPROFOR representatives have been located at objects which were targeted by General Smith yesterday and today." In this next slide we can see more of the conversation. In this particular excerpt it is put directly to Mladic: "Have threats been expressed that these people will be killed? Did you, General Mladic, threaten them like that?" Mladic responded: "General Smith has no right to question me ... I am expecting new air-strikes. I hope that you have been informed that my answer will be the death rattle." Smith and Nikolaj were confused: "I don't know what you are talking about." Mladic then said: "Let him bombard and he will know ..." On the 26th of May, Mladic made direct threats to Smith that he would harm eight UN military observers taken hostage. On the 28th of May, Mladic confirmed to Smith that some of the captured UN personnel were being held at his own headquarters as well as other locations the VRS believed were potential targets of NATO planes. Slide 109 shows this particular passage indicating that Mladic held hostages at his own headquarters in an effort to keep it from being targeted: "General Smith, you are responsible for what has happened. You started killing by NATO aviation ... we are treating UNPROFOR soldiers correctly and humanely. It is true we have placed them at certain locations, starting from my HQ and so on, which we assessed that you would decide to cover in a carpet of NATO bombs. But except for a few cases, we have treated them correctly." The hostages were held until the first -- until the first were released on the 2nd of June, 1995, a process that continued until the 19th of June. Earlier today I spoke about the situation in the eastern enclaves, the UN safe areas. I told you about General Morillon's plea to Mladic to resist the urge to ethnically cleanse them. I told you about Mladic 's threat to David Harland to kill everyone but the children in these eastern enclaves. The next segment of the opening statement, Your Honour, concerns Srebrenica and will be given by Mr. Peter McCloskey. We are ahead of the time that -- we are taking less time than we thought to make our opening statement. And if it's convenient to the Court, we would be able to complete -- adjourn here for the today and complete the remainder of the opening statement tomorrow. Or should the Chamber wish, after a short break, we can rearrange the podium and continue forward today. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. We were informed that Mr. McCloskey would need approximately two hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then for an unspecified time you would deal with some legal matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think approximately 30 to 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that in approximately the first two sessions tomorrow you would be able to conclude?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Possibly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because then if anything would come up which would require further time, practical matters, administrative matters, we would still have time for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe that's the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, under those circumstances, your request that Mr. McCloskey start tomorrow is hereby granted. Before we adjourn, one small observation. Mr. Groome, you now and then quoted from material which was then played after that. Your quotes even when you said you quote literally were not always exactly the same. There was one which I would like to put on the record. At page 56, line 22, you were quoting from a -- what was reported as a conversation in a vehicle Mr. Mladic would have had with Mr. Lesic. The line was: "And whenever I come by Sarajevo I killed." That is how you quoted it. Whereas on page 57, line 13, it's not the past but it's in the present. There it reads: "And whenever I come by Sarajevo, I kill." I'd like to put that on the record. It might be a mistake or a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was just a misstatement, I did intend to say "kill," not the past tense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it was recorded as "killed." Then I'm looking at my colleagues. If there's nothing else at this moment, we can adjourn. We will adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, the 17th of May, at 9.00 in the morning, this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of May, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
